title: Stop Waiting on CI: Shard 160 Tests ⚡
ig_caption:
160 tests… waiting 40 minutes is optional 👀

Here’s what “Parallel CI Test Sharding” does under the hood:
- You split one big test suite into N shards (e.g., 8–32) so work can run simultaneously.
- Serial CI: 1 runner executes everything → feedback arrives late (e.g., “FEEDBACK IN 40 MIN”).
- Sharded CI: multiple runners each run a slice → progress is visible early (e.g., “0/160 DONE → FEEDBACK IN 5 MIN”).
- A coordinator (CI system) assigns tests to shards using a deterministic mapping (by test file/class/case) to avoid duplication.
- Results are collected and merged back into one report so developers see a single source of truth.
- Flaky-risk controls: isolate shared state, limit resource contention, and rerun only the failing shard(s) when needed.

Production takeaway: Shard by stable, deterministic boundaries and design tests to be parallel-safe (no shared mutable state). Start with modest shard counts to find the “best throughput per cost” point.

What’s the real bottleneck in your CI right now: test runtime, environment setup time, or flaky tests?
fb_caption:
Parallel CI Test Sharding is a straightforward idea with real architectural trade-offs: reduce end-to-end feedback time by running independent subsets of tests concurrently, while keeping results correct, deterministic, and operationally resilient.

What happens in the animation:
- Serial pipeline: a single runner processes all tests sequentially. With ~160 tests, the feedback loop can stretch to ~40 minutes.
- Sharded pipeline: the suite is partitioned into shards and distributed across multiple runners. Each runner executes its assigned slice, and the system aggregates results. With enough parallel capacity, you can drive feedback to ~5 minutes.

Key design considerations (the parts that make or break it):
- Shard strategy: Choose stable partition keys (test file/class/case, or tag-based grouping). Avoid random distribution that makes debugging harder.
- Determinism & mapping: A coordinator should consistently map tests to shards so reruns reproduce the same failure set.
- Parallel safety: Tests must not rely on shared mutable state (databases, ports, filesystem paths, global services). Use isolated environments, per-shard namespaces, unique resource identifiers, and teardown discipline.
- Resource contention: Parallelization increases pressure on CPU, memory, network, and external dependencies. Cap concurrency or add circuit breakers to avoid turning CI into a self-inflicted outage.
- Flake containment: Identify flaky tests and quarantine them (or run them with specialized retry/rerun logic per shard) to prevent “false negatives” from poisoning developer trust.

Scalability & resilience:
- Horizontal scaling: Sharding turns a single-workload pipeline into many smaller units that scale with runner availability.
- Failure isolation: When one shard fails, you typically re-run only the affected shard(s), shortening recovery time.
- Observability: Track shard duration variance, queue wait time, and failure rates per shard to spot hotspots and improve partitioning.

Practical best practice: Start with a small number of shards and measure shard runtime distribution—if one shard dominates, your mapping needs refinement. Then ensure environments are parallel-safe before maximizing concurrency.

If you could improve only one thing in your CI tomorrow, would you prioritize faster execution (sharding), faster environment provisioning (caching/images), or higher signal reliability (flake management)?
